documents.content: Eat a balanced diet with plenty of vegetables, fruits, whole grains and protein. Limit salt, sugar and processed foods. Drink at least 8 glasses of clean water daily.
Adults should get about 30 minutes of moderate activity most days, such as brisk walking, cycling or household work. Regular movement improves heart health and mood.
Manage stress with deep breathing, regular sleep, talking to trusted people and taking short breaks. Persistent anxiety or sadness should be discussed with a counsellor.
Aim for 7 to 9 hours of sleep. Keep a regular sleep schedule, avoid screens and caffeine before bed, and keep your bedroom dark and quiet.
Wash a minor cut with clean water, apply gentle pressure to stop bleeding, and cover with a clean bandage. Change the dressing daily and watch for redness or pus.
Cool a minor burn under running water for at least 10 minutes. Do not apply ice, butter or toothpaste. Cover loosely with clean cloth and seek help for large or facial burns.
If someone is choking and cannot breathe or speak, call for emergency help and perform back blows and abdominal thrusts (Heimlich manoeuvre) if trained.
If someone faints, lay them flat, raise their legs slightly, loosen tight clothing and ensure fresh air. If they do not wake quickly, seek urgent medical help.
Wash hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds, especially before eating, after using the toilet, and after coughing or sneezing.
Brush teeth twice a day with fluoride toothpaste and floss once daily. Visit a dentist for check-ups and limit sugary foods and drinks.
Iron-rich foods include leafy greens, legumes, red meat and fortified cereals. Pair them with vitamin C foods like citrus to improve absorption.
Water is essential for every body function. Urine that is pale straw-coloured usually means good hydration; dark urine suggests you need to drink more.
Pregnant women need extra iron, folic acid and protein. Eat iron-rich and fortified foods and attend regular antenatal check-ups.
Breastfeed soon after birth and on demand. Keep the baby warm, sleep the baby on its back, and attend vaccination appointments.
Vaccines protect against serious diseases. Complete the recommended schedule for children and keep up to date with adult boosters as advised by health workers.
Prevent dengue and malaria by removing stagnant water, using bed nets and repellent, and wearing long sleeves, especially at dawn and dusk.
For a fever, rest, drink plenty of fluids and use paracetamol as advised. Seek care if the fever is very high, lasts more than a few days, or comes with a stiff neck or rash.
Symptoms of dehydration include thirst, dark urine, dry mouth and fatigue. Take oral rehydration salts (ORS) and drink small sips of clean water frequently.
High blood pressure often has no symptoms. Follow a low-salt diet, stay active, avoid smoking and take prescribed medication exactly as directed.
Diabetes is managed with a balanced diet, regular activity, monitoring blood sugar and taking medication as prescribed. Attend regular check-ups.
See a doctor for chest pain, difficulty breathing, severe bleeding, high fever, weakness on one side of the body, or symptoms that keep getting worse.
Wash a bite wound with soap and running water, apply antiseptic, and seek care promptly for rabies prevention if the animal's vaccination status is unknown.
Young children need energy-dense foods frequently. Include grains, protein (eggs, pulses, milk), fruits and vegetables and continue breastfeeding for the first two years.
